_readme: Hand-written cards: what a parameter actually does, and what it does ON THE BC-250. 'exact' matches the entry name exactly; 'families' matches by 'starts_with' (a name prefix) or 'contains' (a fragment), for groups of entries that share one explanation. Anything not written here is left blank on purpose: the program says it has no card rather than inventing one. To translate, copy cards/en.json to cards/<language>.json and translate the values only - keys and fragments are firmware entry names and stay in English.

exact.Core Performance Boost:
Opportunistic boost: it lets the cores go above their base frequency when power and temperature allow it. On the BC-250 the decision is not taken by the BIOS but by the SMU, the small power controller inside the APU, which raises and lowers the frequency by itself several times a second.

With 'Auto' (value 1) the boost is on. With 'Disabled' (value 0) the cores are pinned to the base frequency, which lowers heat and consumption and makes benchmarks repeatable, at the cost of single-thread performance.

On a BC-250 running SkillFishOS this setting overlaps with our own work: the P-state tables we inject through ACPI decide which frequency and voltage pairs the kernel may ask for. If you turn the boost off here and then wonder why the CPU is slow under load, this is where to look first.
exact.Downcore control:
How many cores the firmware hands over to the operating system, and in which arrangement. The die inside the BC-250 has eight Zen 2 cores; the stock firmware publishes four.

We do not unlock the other four through this entry: SkillFishOS writes the SMU core mask at register SMN 0x5A870, and skillfish-core-unlock checks whether the mask is already 0xFF and does nothing if it is. The MeiMeiDXEv3 modified firmware does the same job from the firmware side, through its own 'Core Unlock' menu.

'Auto' (value 0) means the firmware decides. The other values name explicit configurations, and their meaning depends on how the cores are grouped in the complex; a value that does not match this silicon can leave the board without cores to boot on.
exact.SMTEN:
Simultaneous multithreading: two hardware threads per core, so four cores appear as eight processors to the operating system.

Turning it off halves the number of visible processors and can raise per-thread performance slightly on workloads that fight over the same core resources; it lowers total throughput on everything that scales with threads. On a machine used for compiling or transcoding, leave it on.

Note for the BC-250: with the core unlock applied you get eight cores, so with SMT on the system sees sixteen processors. Some tools written when the board had four cores make assumptions about that number.
exact.Global C-state Control:
The deep idle states of the cores. With C-states enabled an idle core can stop its clock and, in the deeper states, lose its cached state, waking up in a few microseconds when work arrives.

They are the difference between an idle board that draws a handful of watts and one that draws noticeably more. Turning them off is a debugging measure, not a tuning one: it removes a whole class of wake-up latencies, and it is sometimes done when chasing an instability that appears only when the machine is idle.

On the BC-250 the idle behaviour is also shaped by the P-state tables SkillFishOS injects: if idle consumption looks wrong, check both.
exact.UMA Frame buffer Size:
How much system memory is carved out for the GPU before the operating system boots. On the BC-250 the 16 GB of GDDR6 are shared between CPU and GPU, and this value decides the split.

⚠️ WARNING, measured on the board: this is not the only authority. We wrote UMA_SIZE=4096 in the extended CMOS with our own skillfish-memcfg tool, read it back correctly, and on the next boot the firmware had rewritten the block byte for byte, checksum included. The firmware reasserts its own configuration at every start. So a value set here may or may not survive, and the only proof is a reboot followed by reading the actual value back.

'Auto' is 0xFFFFFFFF and lets the firmware choose. The other values are megabytes: 256M up to 12G. Asking for a huge frame buffer leaves proportionally less memory for the system, and there is no warning if you ask for too much.
exact.IOMMU:
The unit that translates the addresses used by devices doing DMA. It is what makes it possible to hand a PCIe device to a virtual machine safely (VFIO passthrough), and what protects system memory from a device writing where it should not.

On an APU it is not free: address translation adds a step to every DMA transfer, and on some workloads that costs a little bandwidth. 'Auto' is 0xF and lets the firmware decide, which on this board normally means enabled but with the operating system left free to use it or not.

If you plan to pass devices through to virtual machines, this must be on and the kernel must be started with the matching options. If you are chasing a DMA problem that only appears under load, turning it off is a legitimate test - on a board you can still reach.
exact.IOMMU Page Table Format:
Which page table format the IOMMU uses: the older v1 format, the newer v2 format that shares the page tables with the host, or 'Auto'.

It matters for guest memory pinning and for the amount of memory the tables themselves take. 'Auto' is the sensible choice unless a specific hypervisor asks for one of the two; picking a format the rest of the platform does not expect gives errors at boot that name the IOMMU, not this setting.
exact.Memory Clock Speed:
The clock of the GDDR6 memory. On the BC-250 the stock value corresponds to 1750 MHz, and the memory is shared with the GPU, so this number moves both graphics bandwidth and system memory bandwidth at once.

What we have measured on our boards: memory timings are applied only at boot, never hot. Changing them from a running system does nothing, and the value that counts is the one in the APCB block at 0xAB1000 of the flash - the block skillfish-memcfg works on.

⚠️ WARNING: memory is where a wrong value hurts most. Too high a clock does not produce a clear error message: it produces a board that boots sometimes, corrupts data quietly, or hangs during memory training. If you experiment, do it on the development board with the programmer connected.
exact.Above 4G Decoding:
Whether the firmware may place PCI device windows (BARs) above the four gigabyte line. Devices with large memory windows - GPUs above all - need it, and it is the setting that Resizable BAR sits on top of.

On this firmware the entry exists but is hidden by a condition that looks at no variable at all: it is off the menu no matter what you write into any variable. If you need it, the only way is to change the firmware itself.

Note that the BC-250 already has its graphics integrated in the APU, so the usual reason for this setting - a discrete card with a big BAR - does not apply. It matters if you use the PCIe slot for something else.
exact.SR-IOV Support:
Single Root I/O Virtualization: lets one physical PCIe device present itself as several virtual functions, each assignable to a different virtual machine.

It only does something if a device on the bus supports it, and on this board that is unlikely. Like Above 4G Decoding, the entry is present in the firmware but hidden by a condition that no variable can change.
exact.Network Stack:
Whether the firmware brings up its own network stack at boot, which is what PXE and HTTP booting are built on.

This is the single entry whose default differs between the stock P3.00 and the P5.00 'Robin' firmware: stock leaves it off, P5.00 turns it on. All seven network entries that appear in P5.00 and not in the stock - IPv4 and IPv6 PXE, IPv4 and IPv6 HTTP, IP6 configuration policy, PXE wait time, media detect count - appear because of this one flag, not because P5.00 unlocked anything.

Leaving it off shortens boot and removes a network service that runs before any operating system.
exact.Fast Boot:
Skips part of the hardware initialisation to reach the boot loader sooner: fewer device enumerations, less USB probing, no wait for slow disks.

The time it saves is real but modest; what it costs is predictability. With Fast Boot on, a keyboard plugged into the wrong port may not answer during the boot menu, and a disk that spins up slowly may not be seen at all. On a board you administer remotely, and whose BIOS you may need to enter to recover, that is a bad trade.
exact.NB Azalia:
The HD Audio controller in the north bridge - the one that carries audio out over the display connection.

On the BC-250 this is the path through which HDMI or DisplayPort audio reaches a monitor or a TV. Disabling it makes the audio device disappear from the operating system entirely, which is occasionally what you want on a headless machine and is a puzzling loss on any other.
exact.GFX CUs/RB Control:
How many compute units and render back-ends of the GPU the firmware enables.

This matters on the BC-250 more than on most boards: the die carries 40 compute units and the stock configuration does not give them all. We do not take them from here, though - the working route in SkillFishOS is the kernel patch that writes CC_GC_SHADER_ARRAY_CONFIG together with SPI_PG_ENABLE_STATIC_WGP_MASK and RLC_PG_ALWAYS_ON_WGP_MASK. We checked all the BIOS images we have, stock and modified: none of them unlocks the compute units from firmware.

So treat this entry as interesting but unproven. It is hidden in the stock firmware with the defaults it ships with.
exact.NumEncryptedGuests:
The maximum number of virtual machines that can use AMD SEV memory encryption at the same time. Each one needs an ASID, an address space identifier, and the pool is fixed.

Raising it reserves more identifiers and slightly reduces those left for other uses; lowering it means the hypervisor refuses to start encrypted guests past the limit. On a board that is not running encrypted virtual machines the value changes nothing at all.
exact.SEV-ES ASID Space Limit:
Where the identifier space is split between SEV-ES guests, which also encrypt the register state, and plain SEV guests.

It goes together with NumEncryptedGuests, and like it, it has no effect unless something on the machine is actually starting encrypted virtual machines.
exact.Platform First Error Handling:
PFEH decides who sees a correctable hardware error first: the firmware, silently, or the operating system.

With it enabled the firmware absorbs certain machine check events and the operating system never learns about them. That makes logs look clean, and it also makes a memory module that is slowly failing invisible until it fails completely. If you are diagnosing hardware, this is one of the settings to turn off so that Linux gets to see and log the errors itself.
exact.RedirectForReturnDis:
A workaround switch for a processor erratum concerning return address prediction.

It exists to be set by AGESA according to the silicon revision, and 'Auto' means exactly that. There is no performance to be won here, and setting it by hand on a revision that does not need it is a way to spend an afternoon on a very obscure instability.
exact.L2 TLB Associativity:
How the second level translation lookaside buffer is organised. The TLB caches virtual to physical address translations; its associativity changes how often two hot pages evict each other.

Like the erratum switches around it, this is meant to be left on 'Auto': the value that suits the silicon is chosen by AGESA. Changing it is a microarchitectural experiment, measurable only with careful benchmarks and capable of costing performance quietly.
exact.Combo CBS:
A switch internal to AMD's CBS menu that selects which family of settings the rest of the menu applies to. It is scaffolding for a menu shared across several platforms, not a setting for the board.

On the BC-250 it sits at offset 0x000 of the AmdSetup variable, the very first byte, and it is one of the few entries visible in the stock menu tree.
exact.Chipset:
Not a setting: the link that leads from the main menu to the chipset submenus, and from there into the AMD CBS menu with its 1134 entries.

On the stock firmware this link is hidden by a condition that looks at no variable - suppressif TRUE. That is the reason a stock BC-250 shows so little in its BIOS: the entries are all there, and the door to them is bricked up rather than locked. No UEFI variable will open it; only a modified firmware will.
exact.CPU Configuration: The link to the processor submenu. Like Chipset, it is hidden in the stock firmware by a condition that no variable can change.
exact.Advanced CPU Settings: The link to the advanced processor submenu, hidden in the stock firmware by an unconditional suppression, exactly like Chipset and CPU Configuration.
exact.System Date:
The date the firmware keeps in the RTC, the little clock that runs on the battery when the board is off.

On the BC-250 it matters more than it looks: a wrong date makes HTTPS certificates fail to validate, breaks scheduled jobs, and makes log timestamps useless when comparing two machines. Linux normally sets it from the network at every boot, so a date that keeps coming back wrong points at the RTC battery rather than at this entry.
exact.System Time:
The time of day in the RTC. The same as the date: Linux normally corrects it from the network at boot, and a time that drifts badly between one start and the next points at the RTC battery.

Note that the firmware keeps this clock in local time or in UTC depending on how the operating system was installed; a system that shows itself two hours out has an interpretation problem, not a wrong clock.
exact.System Language:
The language the firmware's own menu speaks. It has nothing to do with the operating system's language, and on this board it changes very little: the stock BIOS shows so few entries that there is hardly anything to translate.

It is stored in the standard UEFI variables PlatformLang and PlatformLangCodes, which is why it survives a CMOS clear differently from the rest.
exact.N/A:
An entry the firmware gives no name to: the string identifier points at empty text. It is not a reading mistake of ours - the emulator would say so - it is how the image was built.

Usually these are placeholders left behind by the menu compiler, or entries whose name comes from code at run time. There is nothing to set here, and nothing to learn from the name.
exact:
An entry the firmware gives no name to: the string identifier points at empty text. It is not a reading mistake of ours - the emulator would say so - it is how the image was built.

Usually these are placeholders left behind by the menu compiler, or entries whose name comes from code at run time. There is nothing to set here, and nothing to learn from the name.

families.text:
Clock gating stops the clock of a block of logic while that block has nothing to do. It is one of the main reasons an idle APU draws little power, and it is applied independently to many blocks: the IOMMU levels, the IO hub, the memory hub, the display hub.

These entries exist to be turned off one at a time when chasing a hardware problem: a block that misbehaves when its clock restarts will misbehave less obviously with gating disabled. That is their real purpose. Leaving one disabled costs power for no benefit, and the entries carry no warning about which blocks depend on each other.

On the BC-250 these are hidden in the stock firmware with the shipped defaults.

Medium Grain Clock Gating: the same power saving idea as the other clock gating switches, applied at the granularity of a functional block rather than a whole unit.

They are debugging switches. Turning one off raises idle power and, on paper, removes a class of timing hazards from that block; there is no performance to gain.

A shallow low power state for a specific block, in which it keeps its state but stops most of its activity. Like the clock gating switches nearby, it exists to be turned off while diagnosing, not while tuning.

GRA - Generic Register Access - is a debugging facility of AMD's CBS menu: it lets the firmware read or write an arbitrary hardware register at boot, before the operating system starts. Each group has a full set of entries: the register kind, when to write it, the bus, device and function or the SMN address, the AND mask and the OR value.

⚠️ WARNING. This is the most dangerous thing in the whole menu. There is no validation: the address you write is the address the firmware pokes, at a moment when nothing is up to catch a fault. A wrong write here can stop the board from booting in a way that no setting can undo, because the write happens before the menu you would need to reach.

Use it only with a documented register, on the development board, with the external programmer already connected. The groups are disabled by default, and each group hides its own detail entries until it is enabled.

The UMC is the unified memory controller, the block that drives the GDDR6. These entries expose its configuration registers as raw bit masks: a control entry chooses between 'Auto' and 'Manual', and the individual mask entries below it carry the bits.

They are not documented publicly, and the names say nothing about what each bit does. On the BC-250 the memory configuration that actually applies is the APCB block at 0xAB1000 of the flash, which is what skillfish-memcfg reads and writes.

⚠️ WARNING: memory controller settings are applied during memory training, before anything can report an error. A wrong value shows up as a board that does not finish booting, not as a message.

The USB 3 host controllers and their ports. The BC-250 has two of them, and these entries turn a controller or an individual port on and off, choose link speed limits, and configure overcurrent mapping.

Disabling a controller makes every device on it disappear, keyboard included. On a board you administer over the network that is survivable; on one you are sitting in front of, with the BIOS menu mostly hidden, it is a good way to lock yourself out of your own keyboard.

Part of the IOMMU block: the unit that translates addresses for devices doing DMA. The main switch decides whether the unit exists for the operating system at all; the entries around it size its translation units and page tables.

Unless a hypervisor asks for a specific setting, 'Auto' is what these are meant to be left on.

The mode registers of the GDDR6. Every memory chip has a handful of internal registers - MR0 to MR8 - that set drive strength, termination, read and write latency, refresh behaviour and test modes. These entries let the firmware force a mask and a value into them, per memory pseudo-channel, during memory training.

⚠️ WARNING: nothing here is validated and nothing is documented publicly. These are the settings that decide whether the memory works at all, and they are applied before anything exists that could report an error: a wrong value shows up as a board that never finishes booting, not as a message. On the BC-250 the memory configuration that normally applies comes from the APCB block at 0xAB1000 of the flash, which is what skillfish-memcfg reads and writes.

DFE - Decision Feedback Equalization - on the memory receiver. At GDDR6 speeds the signal arriving at the controller is smeared by the previous bits on the same wire; the DFE subtracts that echo so the sampler sees a clean eye. These entries force the DFE strength per UMC channel instead of leaving it to training.

⚠️ WARNING: these are values that memory training normally measures on the actual board. Forcing them replaces a measurement with a guess, and the failure mode is not a message but data that comes back wrong under load. Change them only on the development board.

Control and mask registers of the UMC, the unified memory controller that drives the GDDR6. They sit in the diagnostic part of the menu: a control entry chooses Auto or Manual, and the mask entries under it carry raw bits with no names and no public documentation.

⚠️ WARNING: like everything else that touches the memory controller, these are applied during memory training, before anything can report a fault. The board either boots or it does not. See also the UMCCONFIG entries, which are the same idea on a different register block.

Voltage offsets for the main rails: VDDCR_VDD feeds the CPU cores, VDDCR_GFX the graphics, VDDCR_SOC the rest of the chip. A control entry enables the offset and a second one carries it in millivolts, applied on top of whatever the SMU asks for.

This is the most useful thing in the debug menu and the easiest to get wrong. On our two BC-250 boards the same undervolt did not hold: the second one computed wrong until it got 40 mV more. Silicon differs board to board, so a value copied from someone else's post is a guess about someone else's chip.

⚠️ WARNING: too little voltage does not crash cleanly. It produces wrong results in compute work, artifacts, and stability that depends on temperature - the kind of fault that costs days to attribute. Change one rail at a time, test under real load, and remember that SkillFishOS already shapes voltage through the injected P-state tables.

PCIe link equalization: rxX_eq_* are the receiver settings (attenuation, VGA gain, boost) and txX_eq_* the transmitter ones (pre-shoot, main cursor, de-emphasis), each set separately for GEN1, GEN2 and GEN3.

They exist because a high speed serial link is shaped by the traces between the two ends. Normally the two ends negotiate these settings themselves at link training; these entries override that negotiation with fixed numbers.

⚠️ WARNING: getting them wrong does not disable the slot cleanly. It gives a link that trains at a lower speed, or one that works until it carries real traffic and then produces correctable errors nobody is looking at. Leave them alone unless you are debugging a specific link with an analyser.

Deep sleep for a specific clock domain: DS_GFXCLK for the graphics clock, DS_SOCCLK for the fabric, DS_LCLK for the IO link, DS_SMNCLK for the management network. These are SMU features: with deep sleep enabled the SMU may drop the clock to a trickle when that domain is idle, instead of merely gating it.

They are on for a reason - they are a large part of why an idle APU is quiet and cool. Turning one off raises idle power and can smooth out a latency spike on that domain; on the BC-250 that trade is rarely worth it, and it is a debugging step, not a tuning one.

The debug unit of the data fabric and of the NBIO. It can send an execution trace into DRAM, or send port 80 codes - the ones a POST card shows - to a chosen destination.

These entries exist for firmware bring-up, not for use. Tracing to DRAM steals memory and bandwidth from the running system, and it is the kind of setting that gets left on by accident and then explains a performance loss nobody can account for.

CCM is the Coherent Master of the data fabric: the port through which the cores reach memory and the rest of the chip while keeping the caches coherent. These entries set link thresholds - when the fabric decides a queue is congested.

They are tuning knobs for AMD's own engineers, with no public units and no documented ranges. On a single-die part like the BC-250 the fabric is not the bottleneck anyway.

Configuration registers of the floating point unit: retirement behaviour, throttling thresholds, x87 handling. They live in the processor debug menu, and they are meant to be poked at by someone chasing an erratum with AMD's own documentation in hand.

There is nothing to gain here and no way to tell that a value is wrong: a floating point unit configured oddly does not report anything, it just computes.

The hardware prefetchers: the logic that guesses which memory line the code will want next and fetches it early. Stream, stride and region prefetchers each guess a different pattern.

Disabling them is a benchmarking measure: on a workload that walks memory unpredictably a prefetcher wastes bandwidth, and on the BC-250 the bandwidth is shared with the GPU. On everything else, turning them off costs performance. Measure before and after, on the same load, or you are just guessing.

DC BTC - Boot Time Calibration of the voltage curve. At every start the firmware measures this particular piece of silicon and works out how much voltage it needs at each frequency. These entries force that calibration instead of letting it run.

⚠️ WARNING: this is the mechanism that makes every board different, and the reason the same undervolt does not hold on two BC-250s - ours needed 40 mV more on the second one. Forcing the calibration replaces a measurement of your own chip with a number, and the failure mode is wrong results rather than a crash.

IOHC - the IO Hub Controller: the block that carries every PCIe lane, the USB controllers and the on-chip devices to the fabric. These entries size its queues, its clock gating and its debug hooks.

On the BC-250 everything that is not CPU or GPU passes through here: the network chip, the NVMe slot, the USB ports. They are AMD bring-up settings, and there is no public documentation for the numbers they take.

USB configuration at chip level: which controllers exist, how their PHY behaves in sleep, and the debug clocks. Different from the entries in the Setup form set, which decide how the firmware itself uses USB during boot.

What matters on a headless board: turning a controller or a PHY off makes the keyboard disappear too. If the BIOS menu is mostly hidden already, that leaves very little room to change your mind.

PCIe settings at the root complex: link speed and width, ASPM power states, hot plug, error reporting. The BC-250 brings one slot out plus the on-board devices.

Forcing a lower link speed is a legitimate way to test a link that misbehaves under load; forcing a higher one than the traces support gives a link that trains and then produces errors nobody is watching. ASPM is the usual suspect when a device disappears after an idle period.
